name: Variables and Operations
description: There are $$$n$$$ variables; let's denote the value of the $$$i$$$-th variable as $$$a_i$$$. There are also $$$m$$$ operations which will be applied to these variables; the $$$i$$$-th operation is described by three integers $$$x_i, y_i, z_i$$$. When the $$$i$$$-th operation is applied, the variable $$$x_i$$$ gets assigned the following value: $$$\min(a_{x_i}, a_{y_i} + z_i)$$$. Every operation will be applied exactly once , but their order is not fixed; they can be applied in any order. Let's call a sequence of initial variable values $$$a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$$$ stable , if no matter in which order we apply operations, the resulting values will be the same. If the resulting value of the $$$i$$$-th variable depends on the order of operations, then the sequence of initial variable values is called $$$i$$$- unstable . You have to process $$$q$$$ queries. In each query, you will be given initial values $$$a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$$$ and an integer $$$k$$$; before applying the operations, you can at most $$$k$$$ times choose a variable and decrease it by $$$1$$$. For every variable $$$i$$$, you have to independently determine if it is possible to transform the given values into an $$$i$$$-unstable sequence.
input_specification: The first line contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$m$$$ ($$$2 \le n \le 500$$$; $$$1 \le m \le 4 \cdot 10^5$$$) — the number of variables and operations, respectively. Then, $$$m$$$ lines follow. The $$$i$$$-th of them contains three integers $$$x_i, y_i, z_i$$$ ($$$1 \le x_i, y_i \le n$$$; $$$x_i \ne y_i$$$; $$$0 \le z_i \le 10^5$$$) — the description of the $$$i$$$-th operation. The next line contains one integer $$$q$$$ ($$$1 \le q \le 1000$$$) — the number of queries. Each query consists of two lines: the first line contains one integer $$$k$$$ ($$$0 \le k \le 10^9$$$) — the maximum number of times you can choose a variable and decrease it by $$$1$$$; the second line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$$$ ($$$0 \le a_i \le 10^9$$$) — the initial values of the variables.
output_specification: For each query, print a string of $$$n$$$ zeroes and/or ones. The $$$i$$$-th character should be 1 if it is possible to obtain an $$$i$$$-unstable sequence, or 0 otherwise.
approach_summary: Formulate the state transition graph with non-negative weights. Execute Dijkstra's algorithm with priority queue to find shortest paths in O((V + E) log V).

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 2112F — Variables and Operations [168. Dijkstra's Algorithm]
topic_editorial.summary: Single-source shortest path using Dijkstra's algorithm.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: Because all edge weights are non-negative, the shortest distance to the unvisited vertex with the minimum tentative distance is finalized and cannot be decreased by further transitions (greedy choice property).
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Graph Modeling
Construct an adjacency list with pairs $(v, w)$ for each directed or undirected edge from $u$ to $v$ with weight $w \ge 0$.

### Step 2: Distance Table Initialization
Initialize $dist[v] = \infty$ for all vertices, with $dist[\text{source}] = 0$.
Push $(0, \text{source})$ into a min-priority queue `std::priority_queue<pair<long long, int>, vector<pair<long long, int>>, greater<>>`.

### Step 3: Relaxation Loop
While the priority queue is not empty:
1. Pop $(d, u)$. If $d > dist[u]$, discard (stale entry).
2. For each neighbor $(v, w)$ of $u$:
   If $dist[u] + w < dist[v]$:
   $$dist[v] = dist[u] + w$$
   Push $(dist[v], v)$ into the priority queue.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((V + E) \log V)$
  Every vertex is extracted from the priority queue at most once. For every edge, we perform at most one priority queue push operation taking $\mathcal{O}(\log V)$.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(V + E)$
  Required for storing the adjacency list and the distance array.
